We have mass spec: m/z 193.1103 (intensity 100) as base peak. Likely molecular ion. The formula from candidate COc1ccccc1C(=O)NCCC gave C11H15NO2. Let's calculate exact mass: C11H15NO2 = 11*12.0000 + 15*1.007825 + 14.00307 + 2*15.994915 = 132 + 15.117375 + 14.00307 + 31.98983 = 193.110275 approx. That matches m/z 193.1102787. So formula matches. Good.

Now we have proton NMR data: peaks: 1.20 (d, J=7.1 Hz, 3H) likely ethyl CH3 attached to CH (maybe part of N-CH-CH3? Actually 1.20 d 3H suggests CH3 coupled to CH (quartet). 2.85 (d, 2H) maybe CH2 next to carbonyl? 3.09 (qdd, 1H) maybe CH attached to CH3 and CH2? 3.81 (s, 3H) methoxy on aromatic. Aromatic: 7.15 ddd 2H, 7.92 ddd 2H typical para-disubstituted anisole? Actually anisole (methoxy phenyl) has 4 aromatic protons as AA'BB' pattern: two doublets. Here we have two ddd each 2H, maybe due to ortho and meta couplings with substituent at para? The pattern matches para-substituted anisole (para- substituted). So aromatic ring has methoxy and carbonyl attached at para positions? The SMILES COc1ccccc1C(=O)NCCC is anisole with carbonyl attached at para? Actually COc1ccccc1C(=O)NCCC: methoxy at position 1, carbonyl at position attached to same carbon as methoxy? The SMILES: COc1ccccc1C(=O)NCCC means anisole with carbonyl attached to same carbon as methoxy? That would be ortho? Let's parse: COc1ccccc1 is anisole (methoxy attached to aromatic carbon). Then C(=O)NCCC attached to that aromatic carbon (the same carbon as the methoxy? Actually after the aromatic closure, we have C(=O)NCCC attached to the aromatic carbon after the ring, meaning the carbon attached to the aromatic carbon is carbonyl carbon attached to the ring (i.e., aryl ketone). So we have anisole with para? Not necessarily. The pattern of aromatic protons: 4 protons, two sets of 2H each, suggests para-disubstituted benzene (symmetrical). In anisole (methoxy) alone, you have 5 aromatic protons. Adding another substituent at para gives 4 protons symmetrical. So the structure is p-methoxybenzoyl amide? Actually p-methoxybenzoyl amide: 4-methoxybenzoyl amide (p-anisoyl amide). The carbonyl attached to aromatic ring (benzoyl) and methoxy at para. That matches SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCCC (para). The SMILES we validated earlier is COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCCC (para). The earlier SMILES COc1ccccc1C(=O)NCCC is same but unspecified substitution pattern; but the aromatic pattern suggests para.

Our candidate SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCCC. Let's compute formula: same C11H15NO2. Good.

Now we have NMR: 1.20 d (3H) and 3.09 qdd (1H) and 2.85 d (2H). This suggests an ethyl group attached to nitrogen? Actually N-CH2-CH3 would give CH3 doublet (if CH2 is adjacent to CH3 and CH2 is attached to N? Typically N-CH2-CH3 gives CH3 triplet (J~7) and CH2 quartet. But we have CH3 doublet, CH (quartet?), CH2 doublet. So maybe we have -CH(CH3)-CH2-? The pattern: CH3 doublet (coupled to CH), CH (quartet) coupled to CH3 and CH2 (qdd), CH2 doublet (coupled to CH). So chain is -CH(CH3)-CH2- attached to carbonyl N? Actually N attached to CH (bearing CH3) and CH2? The SMILES NCCC indicates N attached to CH2-CH2-CH3? Wait NCCC is N-CH2-CH2-CH3 (propyl). That would give CH3 triplet, CH2 quartet, CH2 multiplet. Not matching.

Our NMR suggests N attached to CH (bearing CH3) and CH2? Could be N-CH(CH3)-CH2-? That's isobutyl amide: N-CH(CH3)-CH2-? Actually isobutyl: -CH2-CH(CH3)2 gives doublet of doublet? Not.

Let's examine: 1.20 d (3H) J=7.1 suggests CH3 coupled to a CH (single neighbor). 3.09 qdd (1H) J=7.1,6.9,6.9 suggests CH coupled to CH3 and two CH2? Actually qdd indicates coupling to three protons: one large J 7.1 (to CH3) and two ~6.9 (to two equivalent protons maybe CH2). So CH is attached to CH3 and CH2 (two protons). So CH is CH attached to CH3 and CH2 (i.e., CH-CH3 and CH-CH2). That is a CH in a -CH-CH3-CH2- fragment (like CH attached to both CH3 and CH2). That is a 2-butanol type but here attached to N? The CH2 doublet at 2.85 (d, J=6.9) suggests CH2 coupled only to that CH (one neighbor). So we have -CH2-CH(-CH3)-? The CH2 is attached to carbonyl? Actually carbonyl adjacent CH2 would be CH2 next to carbonyl (alpha to carbonyl) which appears around 2.5-3.0 ppm, doublet if coupled to CH? Could be CH2 adjacent to carbonyl and attached to CH (which is attached to N). So structure: N-CH(-CH3)-CH2-C(=O)-Ar? Wait carbonyl attached to aromatic ring, not to chain. The chain is N-CH(-CH3)-CH2-? Actually N attached to carbonyl (amide). So N is part of amide: C(=O)N-... The N is attached to carbonyl and to side chain. The side chain is propyl? In our SMILES, N attached to CH2-CH2-CH3 (propyl). That would give CH3 triplet, CH2 quartet, CH2 multiplet. Not match.

Alternative: N attached to CH(CH3)-CH2- (i.e., isobutyl amide). SMILES: C(=O)NCC(C)C? Actually isobutyl: -CH2-CH(CH3)2. That gives CH3 doublet? No, isobutyl has two equivalent CH3 doublets? Actually CH3 attached to CH (which is attached to CH2). The CH3 appear as doublet (J~6-7). The CH appears as multiplet (septet). The CH2 appears as multiplet. So pattern matches: CH3 doublet (3H), CH (septet) maybe appears as qdd, CH2 doublet? CH2 would be coupled to CH (3 protons) giving quartet? Not doublet. But CH2 adjacent to carbonyl (alpha) would be deshielded ~2.8 ppm, and coupling to CH (3J) maybe 7 Hz, giving quartet (if CH has 1 H). But we see doublet for CH2, meaning only one neighbor? That suggests CH2 is attached to CH (1 H) and maybe not to other protons. So CH2 is attached to CH (1 H) and carbonyl? Actually CH2 attached to carbonyl (C=O) and CH (1 H). That would give doublet (coupling to CH). So chain: CH2-CH(-CH3)-C(=O)-Ar? But carbonyl is attached to aromatic ring, not to chain. Wait we have amide: Ar-CO-N-CH(-CH3)-CH2? That would be N attached to CH(-CH3)-CH2. The carbonyl is attached to aromatic ring, not to chain. So the CH2 is attached to N (not carbonyl). N-CH2-CH(CH3)-? Actually N attached to CH2 (2H) which is attached to CH (1H) which has CH3. That would give CH2 doublet (coupled to CH), CH (quartet) coupled to CH2 and CH3, CH3 doublet. That matches observed: CH2 at 2.85 d (2H) (adjacent to N, deshielded ~2.8), CH at 3.09 qdd (1H) (adjacent to CH2 and CH3), CH3 at 1.20 d (3H). So side chain is N-CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., N-CH2-CH(CH3)-). The other side of N is carbonyl attached to aromatic ring. So the amide is N-(1-methylethyl) (i.e., isopropyl?) Wait N-CH2-CH(CH3)- is 2-aminopropyl? Actually N-CH2-CH(CH3)- is 2-aminopropyl? The chain is -CH2-CH(CH3)- (2-aminopropyl). So the amide is N-(2-aminopropyl)?? But the N is part of amide, so it's N-(2-aminopropyl)benzamide? Actually the amide nitrogen is attached to carbonyl and to CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., 2-aminopropyl). So the SMILES would be COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCC(C)C? Wait N attached to CH2-CH(CH3)-? That's N-CH2-CH(CH3)-? That's N-CH2-CH(CH3)-? The terminal carbon is CH3 attached to CH (which also attached to CH2). So chain length 2 carbons after N: CH2-CH(CH3). That's N-CH2-CH(CH3). So SMILES: ...C(=O)NCC(C) . That is N-CH2-CH(CH3). That's C(=O)NCC(C). That gives formula C? Let's compute: aromatic C7H? plus methoxy OCH3 adds OCH3. Let's compute formula for COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCC(C). Atoms: aromatic ring C6H4 (since two substituents). plus methoxy OCH3 adds C1 H3 O1. plus carbonyl C=O adds C1 O1. plus amide N adds N1. plus side chain: CH2-CH(CH3) = C2 H5. Total C: 6+1+1+2 =10? Wait aromatic ring C6, plus carbonyl carbon 1 =7, plus methoxy carbon 1 =8, plus side chain carbons 2 =10. But we need C11 per formula. Actually aromatic ring with two substituents still C6, but we also have carbonyl carbon attached to ring (makes C7). Methoxy carbon adds 1 (C8). Side chain adds 2 (C10). That's only 10. But formula earlier C11. Did we miss something? The aromatic ring also includes the carbon bearing carbonyl (part of ring). Already counted. So total C10. But mass spec indicates C11. So maybe side chain is three carbons: N-CH2-CH2-CH3 (propyl) gives C3 side chain, total C11. But NMR didn't match. However maybe the CH2 doublet is actually CH2 adjacent to carbonyl (alpha) not N. Let's reconsider original SMILES COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCCC (propyl amide). N attached to propyl chain: N-CH2-CH2-CH3. NMR for propyl amide: CH3 triplet ~1.0, CH2 quartet ~2.0? Actually N-CH2-CH2-CH3: the terminal CH3 couples to CH2 (triplet). The middle CH2 couples to CH3 and CH2 (quartet). The N-CH2 couples to middle CH2 (triplet). So we would see triplet at ~1.0 (3H), quartet at ~2.0 (2H), triplet at ~3.2 (2H). Not matching observed. Observed: only one CH3 doublet, not triplet. So propyl not correct.

Thus the formula C11H15NO2 must be correct. Let's compute formula for COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCC(C)C (isobutyl amide). That side chain is N-CH2-CH(CH3)2 (isobutyl). Carbons: aromatic 6, carbonyl 1 =7, methoxy 1 =8, side chain: CH2 (1) + CH (1) + two CH3 (2) =4 carbons, total C12. Too many.

What about N-CH(CH3)-CH3 (ethyl isopropyl?) That's N-CH(CH3)CH3 (isopropyl). Side chain C3. Total C11? aromatic 6 + carbonyl 1 + methoxy 1 + side chain 3 =11. Good. Structure: N attached to carbonyl and to isopropyl group (i.e., N-isopropyl amide). SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)N(C)C? Wait isopropyl is -CH(CH3)2 attached to N. That's N-isopropyl. SMILES: C(C)C? Actually isopropyl attached via N to carbon: N(C(C)C). So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NC(C)C. Let's compute NMR: isopropyl group gives a doublet for 6H (two CH3) and a septet for 1H (CH). But observed only one CH3 doublet (3H) not 6H. So not isopropyl.

Thus the side chain must be N-CH2-CH(CH3)-? That's N-CH2-CH(CH3)-? That's 2 carbons after N plus one extra CH3 = total 3 carbons side chain, C10? Wait side chain carbons: CH2 (1) + CH (1) + CH3 (1) =3. So total C11. Good. So side chain is N-CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., N-(1-methylethyl)?? Actually that's N-(1-methylethyl)?? The group is 2-aminopropyl? But attached to N, it's N-CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., N-(1-methylethyl)?? The group is N-CH2-CH(CH3)- (propyl with branching at the end). That's called N-(1-methylethyl)ethyl? Not standard. The SMILES: C(=O)NCC(C) . That's carbonyl attached to N, N attached to CH2-CH(CH3). So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCC(C). Let's compute formula: aromatic 6, carbonyl 1 =7, methoxy 1 =8, side chain: CH2 (1) + CH (1) + CH3 (1) =3 => total C11. Hydrogens: aromatic ring 4 (since two substituents), methoxy 3, carbonyl none, side chain: CH2 2, CH 1, CH3 3 =6. Total H =4+3+6=13? plus maybe amide NH? The N has H? In SMILES N attached to carbonyl and CH2, so N has H (since not substituted). So add 1 H =14. But formula earlier C11H15NO2 includes 15 H. We have 14. Let's recount: aromatic ring with two substituents (para) has 4 H. Yes. Methoxy OCH3 adds 3 H. Side chain CH2 2 H, CH 1 H, CH3 3 H =6. NH 1 H. Total =4+3+6+1=14. So missing one H. Maybe aromatic ring is not para but ortho giving 5 aromatic H? That would give 5+3+6+1=15. But aromatic pattern shows 4 protons symmetrical. So maybe the amide nitrogen is N-methyl? Actually N has no H, but side chain includes extra CH3? Let's try N-methylpropyl? Not.

Our earlier candidate COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCCC gave formula C11H15NO2 (matches). N has no H (since attached to carbonyl and propyl chain). Propyl chain CH2-CH2-CH3 gives 7 H (2+2+3). Aromatic 4 H, methoxy 3 H =14, plus maybe NH? No NH. So total 14? Wait compute: aromatic 4, methoxy 3 =7, propyl 7 =14. Need 15. So there is an extra H somewhere: maybe aromatic has 5 H (monosubstituted) but we have two substituents. Let's compute formula for COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCCC using RDKit gave C11H15NO2. So my manual count off. Let's trust RDKit.

Thus the propyl amide matches formula and mass. But NMR didn't match typical pattern? Let's examine the NMR data again: 1.20 d (3H) suggests CH3 doublet, not triplet. Could be due to CH3 attached to CH2 that is attached to carbonyl (alpha to carbonyl) which can be diastereotopic? But coupling pattern for CH3-CH2- is triplet, not doublet. Doublet suggests CH3 attached to CH (single neighbor). So maybe the chain is -CH(CH3)-CH2-? That would be CH3 doublet, CH (quartet), CH2 doublet. That matches observed. So side chain is CH2-CH(CH3)- attached to N? Which orientation? N attached to CH2 (alpha) which is attached to CH (beta) which has CH3. So N-CH2-CH(CH3)-? That's N-CH2-CH(CH3)-? The terminal CH maybe attached to something else? In our molecule, after CH(CH3)- there is nothing (just CH3). So chain length 2 after N. That's N-CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., N-(1-methylethyl)??). That matches formula C11H15NO2? Let's compute: aromatic 6, carbonyl 1 =7, methoxy 1 =8, side chain carbons: CH2 (1), CH (1), CH3 (1) =3 => total C11. Hydrogens: aromatic 4, methoxy 3 =7, side chain: CH2 2, CH 1, CH3 3 =6, plus NH? N attached to carbonyl and CH2, so N has H (since not substituted). So +1 =14? Wait N has H? In SMILES N attached to carbonyl and CH2, so N has one H. So total H =7+6+1=14. Still missing one. Maybe aromatic has 5 H (monosubstituted) but we have two substituents. Something off.
